expectedText:
MOVE-AWAY CUSTODY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Casey Lee · Jordan Lee

RELOCATION NOTICE AND BASIC INFORMATION
This Move-Away Custody Information Sheet concerns Casey Lee, whose parents are Jordan Lee and Taylor Morgan, subject to an existing or contemplated custody arrangement associated with San Francisco County. The proposed new residence address identified for Casey Lee is: Portland, Oregon. The proposed date of the move identified is: December 1, 2026. The reason identified for the proposed move is: new job opportunity. This notice is dated October 1, 2026. This document records the notice information described above for reference alongside an existing custody order, a pending custody proceeding, or the parents' own negotiation. It is not itself a court order, a court filing, or a determination of any party's rights, and completing it does not itself authorize, restrain, or resolve the proposed relocation. Whether a court-ordered notice term already applies to Casey Lee's parents, what notice period or procedure it requires, and what county-specific local forms or rules apply, depend on the terms of any existing custody order and are not supplied by this document.

THE FAMILY CODE'S RELOCATION RIGHT AND THE COURT'S POWER TO RESTRAIN IT
California's move-away framework starts from a general statute, not a custody-specific one: a parent entitled to custody of a child has a right to change the child's residence, subject to the power of the court to restrain a removal that would prejudice the child's rights or welfare. That statute does more than state a bare right. In the same section, the Legislature separately declared its intent to affirm a specific California Supreme Court decision, In re Marriage of Burgess (1996) 13 Cal.4th 25, and to make that decision's rule the declared public policy and law of the state. The statute's structure -- a right to relocate, an express carve-out for a court's power to restrain a prejudicial move, and a legislative endorsement of a named judicial decision -- is what makes the case law discussed elsewhere in this document (rather than freestanding policy argument) the operative gloss on how the restraint power is actually exercised for Casey Lee, whose parents are Jordan Lee and Taylor Morgan.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A parent entitled to the custody of a child has a right to change the residence of the child, subject to the power of the court to restrain a removal that would prejudice the rights or welfare of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 7501(a) (California Legislative Information text), the presumptive relocation right and the court's power to restrain it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7501.)
  "It is the intent of the Legislature to affirm the decision in In re Marriage of Burgess (1996) 13 Cal.4th 25, and to declare that ruling to be the public policy and law of this state."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 7501(b) (California Legislative Information text), the Legislature's stated intent to affirm Burgess as state policy and law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7501.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific presumptive relocation right for a parent entitled to custody, expressly subject to a court's power to restrain a prejudicial move -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific relocation dispute, and not a claim that this right is unconditional or self-executing. This provision sits in Division 12 (Parent and Child Relationship) of the Family Code, a different division than the custody definitions, best-interest standard, and joint-custody provisions cited elsewhere in this document's companion clauses, which sit in Division 8 (Custody of Children). This is a single statutory section (Section 7501, both subdivisions); no additional independent statutory source was found for the relocation right itself. This corpus's Parenting Plan document independently cites the same section (clause parenting_relocation) for its own, briefer purpose; it is cited again here, independently re-verified against the statute's live text on the date above, for this document's deeper treatment of the same right and the case law it points to.

THE NOTICE REQUIREMENT DEPENDS ON THE CUSTODY ORDER, NOT ON A STATEWIDE DEFAULT
California does not impose a single, automatic statewide notice period before every relocation. Instead, one Family Code section authorizes a California court, when making a custody order, to include a notice term in that order: the court may specify that a parent shall notify the other parent if the parent plans to change the residence of the child for more than 30 days, unless the parents have a prior written agreement to the removal. Where such a term exists in an order, the statute describes how and when notice is to be given: before the contemplated move, by mail, return receipt requested, postage prepaid, to the other parent's last known address, with a copy to that parent's counsel of record, and -- to the extent feasible -- provided at least 45 days before the proposed change of residence so as to allow time for mediation of a new custody agreement. Whether a notice term of this kind applies to Casey Lee's parents, Jordan Lee and Taylor Morgan, therefore depends on whether their own custody order in San Francisco County (or elsewhere) actually contains one -- not on this statute alone.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In making an order for custody, if the court does not consider it inappropriate, the court may specify that a parent shall notify the other parent if the parent plans to change the residence of the child for more than 30 days, unless there is prior written agreement to the removal."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 3024 (California Legislative Information text), the court-authorized notice term and its content, timing, and method (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3024.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, court-order-contingent notice mechanism -- not a claim that California law requires advance notice of every relocation in every case, and not a claim about which state's law governs a specific custody matter. The statute is framed as a grant of authority to the court ("the court may specify"), not as a self-executing duty on every parent; a parent's actual notice obligation, if any, comes from the specific custody order a court has entered, or from the parents' own prior written agreement, not from this section standing alone. This is a single statutory section (Section 3024); no additional independent source was found for it, and no California Rule of Court imposing a separate, freestanding move-away notice requirement was independently verified for this document. This section also does not apply to custody orders made before January 1, 1989, a limitation this clause does not further explore because it is unlikely to affect a current relocation dispute.

A COURT-ORDERED CUSTODY EVALUATION'S REPORT IS CONFIDENTIAL
A contested move-away dispute is, procedurally, a child custody proceeding, and California law contains a general rule that applies to any such proceeding, not only to relocation disputes: if a report containing psychological evaluations of a child, or recommendations regarding the child's custody or visitation, is submitted to the court -- including, but not limited to, a report prepared under the Family Code chapter governing court-appointed child custody evaluations -- that report must be placed in the confidential portion of the court file and may not be disclosed except to a limited list of persons: a party and the party's attorney, specified law enforcement, licensing, judicial, court, or family court facilitator personnel acting within the scope of their duties, counsel appointed for the child, or any other person on a court order for good cause. Where a court orders a custody evaluation in connection with Casey Lee's parents' move-away dispute, this confidentiality rule -- not a general assumption that court records are public -- governs who may see the resulting report.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In a proceeding involving child custody or visitation rights, if a report containing psychological evaluations of a child or recommendations regarding custody of, or visitation with, a child is submitted to the court, including, but not limited to, a report created pursuant to Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 3110) of this part and a recommendation made to the court pursuant to Section 3183, that information shall be contained in a document that shall be placed in the confidential portion of the court file of the proceeding, and may not be disclosed, except to the following persons: (1) A party to the proceeding and the party’s attorney. (2) A federal or state law enforcement officer, the licensing entity of a child custody evaluator, a judicial officer, court employee, or family court facilitator of the superior court of the county in which the action was filed, or an employee or agent of that facilitator, acting within the scope of the facilitator’s duties. (3) Counsel appointed for the child pursuant to Section 3150. (4) Any other person upon order of the court for good cause."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 3025.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), the confidentiality of custody-evaluation and recommendation reports, and the limited list of persons who may see them (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3025.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific confidentiality rule for evaluation and recommendation reports submitted in a child custody or visitation proceeding -- not a claim that every move-away dispute involves a custody evaluation, and not a claim about which state's law governs a specific proceeding. This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of Section 3025.5; subdivision (b), which separately addresses confidentiality of information disclosed to a custody evaluator's licensing entity for professional-conduct investigations, is not restated here. This document does not independently verify the custody-evaluation procedure itself (Family Code Section 3111 and the surrounding chapter, referenced in this section but not separately fetched or quoted here) -- only the confidentiality rule that applies once such a report exists. This is a single statutory section; no additional independent source was found for it.

BACKGROUND ON THE CONTESTED MOVE-AWAY STANDARD AND JOINT-CUSTODY CASES
Beyond the statutory right described elsewhere in this document, California's move-away rules are substantially shaped by case law that this document does not independently verify against the primary court opinions and therefore does not cite as legal authority. Family-law commentary and secondary sources widely report that where one parent has sole or primary physical custody, the parent opposing a proposed move bears the burden of showing the move would cause detriment to Casey Lee, at which point a court weighs the child's best interest using a multi-factor inquiry -- commonly summarized as including the child's need for stability and continuity, the distance of the move, the child's age, the child's relationship with each parent, the parents' ability to communicate and cooperate, the child's own wishes if the child is mature enough, the reasons given for the move, and the extent to which custody is currently shared -- and that this framework, and the presumption that precedes it, is reported to apply differently, or not to apply in the same form, where the parents instead share joint physical custody rather than one parent holding sole or primary physical custody. Because this document has not independently confirmed this description against the text of the underlying court opinions, Jordan Lee and Taylor Morgan should not rely on the summary above as a citation-quality statement of the law, and should instead consult the actual case law -- or an attorney -- for Casey Lee's specific situation, particularly to confirm which presumption, if any, applies to their own custody arrangement.

SIGNATURE AND CERTIFICATION — NOT A COURT ORDER
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing information is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on October 1, 2026 at San Francisco, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

Signature of Taylor Morgan (if acknowledging receipt): ☐ _________________________

[This Move-Away Custody Information Sheet is prepared for informational reference concerning a proposed change in Casey Lee's residence. It does not constitute legal advice, a court filing, or a determination of any party's rights under California's move-away law, and it does not itself authorize, restrain, modify, or resolve any custody order or proposed relocation; only a court order, or the parents' own agreement incorporated into one, can do that.]
